dialogue.text: [serious, engaging] In our scenario, the first big bank to go is in Europe. It lent heavily to AI data centers, and on a Monday morning its customers find the doors locked.
We're open again Wednesday. I'm sorry. No, I don't know if that's true.

[serious, engaging] Here's the honest answer for your own account. In America, the government insures up to two hundred and fifty thousand dollars per person at each bank, and when a bank fails, people usually get that money back within days. In Europe, it's a hundred thousand euros.

[serious, engaging] But the insurance doesn't protect your paycheck. In March 2023, Silicon Valley Bank collapsed over a weekend, and thousands of companies had their payroll money inside it. For a few days, a lot of workers had no idea whether Friday's paycheck would arrive.

[serious, engaging] And one bank is how the last world depression spread. The crash of 1929 started in New York, but in 1931, Austria's biggest bank, the Creditanstalt in Vienna, collapsed, and the panic ran across Europe until Germany closed all of its banks by law.
[serious, engaging] Month three. Your fund slides to seven thousand five hundred, and the crash shows up on your grocery receipt.

[serious, engaging] Every country starts protecting itself. Governments put taxes on foreign goods, and you pay those taxes at the checkout. Some countries stop selling their food abroad, like India did in 2023, when the world's biggest rice seller banned most of its rice exports and rice prices around the world jumped.
